teaser: Two grinning demons, a lot of empty gold, and three centuries of painters copying them.

lesson.text: Some eighty years after these two screens were painted, a Kyoto artist named Ogata Kōrin stood in front of them and copied them, figure for figure. A century after that, a painter in Edo named Sakai Hōitsu copied Kōrin's copy. Three artists who never met, born about a hundred years apart, all painting the same two gods.

The original is by Tawaraya Sōtatsu, and almost nothing about him is certain. No birth date, no death date. He ran a Kyoto shop called Tawaraya that sold painted fans and decorated papers, and he rose from shopkeeper to painter of temples. He did not even sign this work.

What he left is a pair of two-panel folding screens, each roughly 1.5 meters high and 1.7 wide (about 5 by 5 and a half feet), covered in squares of gold leaf. On the gold, two creatures. Meet them one at a time.

lesson.title: Who is who
lesson.text: Two gods rush in from the outer edges. Begin on the left.

spots.title: Raijin, thunder
spots.text: White skin, horns, a headband, a wide grin. Raijin is the god of thunder. In each fist he grips a short stick with two round ends, raised to strike.

spots.title: His drums
spots.text: Small drums are strung on a hoop around him like beads. Every blow of the sticks is a clap of thunder. That is where the noise in the sky comes from.

spots.title: Fūjin, wind
spots.text: Green skin, a horn, hair blown straight back, teeth bared. Fūjin is the god of wind, running in on a dark cloud.

spots.title: The bag of winds
spots.text: The white arc over his head is a long sack, held shut at both ends in his fists. All the winds are inside. He loosens his grip and a gale escapes.

lesson.text: So these are the weather. In Buddhist temples the pair usually appeared as small attendants at the feet of a greater deity, guards at the edge of the scene. Sōtatsu's bold move was to throw out the main figure and give the two helpers the whole stage.

His likely models were not paintings at all. In the Kyoto temple hall of Sanjūsangen-dō stand two fierce wooden statues of the wind and thunder gods, carved in the thirteenth century. Sōtatsu seems to have turned sculpture back into flat, flying shapes.

He also changed a color. Thunder gods were traditionally painted red. Here Raijin is chalk white, which makes him flash against the gold like lightning, and balances the white sack on the other side. Now notice where the two of them are placed, and what sits between.
The composition is built on what is missing. Three lines show it.

lines.label: The empty middle
lines.text: Nearly half the surface is bare gold. No landscape, no horizon. The gods are pushed to the outer edges, so the center becomes open sky waiting for a storm.

lines.label: Raijin looks down
lines.text: The thunder god's eyes point down and across, toward the ground far below. He is higher than his partner, about to drop.

lines.label: Fūjin looks across
lines.text: The wind god stares leftward into the gap. The two gazes aim at the same emptiness without meeting, which keeps your own eye swinging between them.

lesson.text: Sōtatsu makes empty gold the main event. The storm has not happened yet: it is about to break in the space between the two gods.

The gold is real: thin beaten squares, laid one by one, whose joins you can still make out as a faint grid. In a dim room lit by lamps it would have glowed and shifted as you moved. And Sōtatsu lets his figures burst out of this precious field, as if it were too small for them.
Raijin's hoop of drums does not fit inside the picture. Where does it slip out of the frame?

spots.title: Cut by the edge
spots.text: At the top, the hoop runs off the screen and comes back. Fūjin's scarf does the same on the far right. Cropping makes the gods feel caught mid-flight, larger than their frame.

lesson.text: That trick of cutting a figure with the border feels modern, like a snapshot. It was daring in the 1600s. So were the clouds: not outlined, but made of ink pooled on a wet surface and left to spread by itself. The method is called tarashikomi, “dripping in”, and Sōtatsu is credited with inventing it.

When Hōitsu owned Kōrin's copy, he painted on its back. Behind the thunder god he put summer grasses beaten by rain, and behind the wind god, autumn vines tossed by a gust. The backs answer the fronts.

spots.title: Ink cloud
spots.text: No outline anywhere. Dark ink was dropped into wet ink and allowed to bloom, leaving soft edges and blotches. The cloud looks like smoke because it was half painted by accident.

spots.title: Flying scarf
spots.text: A dark ribbon with a white lining whips out to the right. Its S-curves are the only thing reaching toward the empty center, like a trail of speed.

spots.title: A belly button
spots.text: Raijin's navel is drawn as a little sunburst. In Japanese folklore, children are told to cover their bellies in a storm, or the thunder god will steal their navels.

spots.title: Running foot
spots.text: Fūjin's clawed foot lands on the cloud, an anklet ringing his leg. The bent knees and spread toes belong to a sprinter, not a statue.

spots.title: Bare gold
spots.text: Look for the faint grid of squares. Each one is a single sheet of beaten gold, thinner than paper, pressed on by hand.

spots.title: The drumstick
spots.text: A stubby stick with a black knob at each end. One arm is up, one is down: he is in the middle of a drum roll.

lesson.text: The screens belong to Kennin-ji, the oldest Zen temple in Kyoto, though the original is kept for safety at the Kyoto National Museum and the temple shows a faithful replica. They are a National Treasure of Japan.
The two gods never retired. They guard the famous Kaminarimon, the “Thunder Gate” of Sensō-ji temple in Tokyo, one in each side bay, where millions of visitors walk between them every year.

As for the chain of copies, it had no teacher at its start and no classroom. Kōrin never met Sōtatsu. Hōitsu never met Kōrin. Each simply saw something he could not leave alone, and painted it again. That is one honest way to measure a picture: by how many people have needed to redo it.

quiz.question: What does the white arc above the green god represent?
quiz.explanation: Fūjin holds a long bag of winds shut at both ends.

quiz.question: How does Raijin make thunder?
options: By beating a ring of drums
quiz.explanation: He strikes the small drums strung on a hoop around him.

quiz.question: What occupies the center of the composition?
quiz.explanation: Sōtatsu pushed both gods to the edges and left the middle bare.

quiz.question: What is tarashikomi?
options: Dropping ink or color into a still-wet area so it pools and spreads
Copying an older painting line for line
quiz.explanation: The word means “dripping in”; Sōtatsu used it for the clouds.

quiz.question: Who copied these screens about eighty years later?
quiz.explanation: Kōrin copied Sōtatsu; Hōitsu later copied Kōrin's version.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the color of Sōtatsu's thunder god?
options: He is white instead of the traditional red
He is gold like the background
quiz.explanation: Thunder gods were usually red; this one is chalk white.

facts.text: Sōtatsu signed and dated the screens in the lower corner.
facts.explanation: The work carries no signature, and even the painter's dates are unknown.

facts.text: Parts of the drum hoop and the scarf are cut off by the edge of the screens.
facts.explanation: Sōtatsu crops them so the gods seem too big and too fast for the frame.

facts.text: Before becoming a temple painter, Sōtatsu ran a shop selling painted fans.
facts.explanation: His Kyoto shop, Tawaraya, sold fans and decorated papers.
